introduction: “The creation of God embraceth worlds besides this world, and creatures apart from these creatures.” Bahá’u’lláh affirmed that every fixed star has its planets and every planet its creatures; ‘Abdu’l-Bahá argued that so vast a creation cannot be empty; and the guide adds the ancient philosophers who held that a good source must overflow into every possible form of life. Later letters caution that nothing is said about what such creatures are like. The Qur’an speaks of living things dispersed through the heavens and the earth, the Psalmist and Kant of awe before the stars, and Pope’s “vast chain of being” is the classical doctrine of plenitude that readings 33 to 38 quote at its source. Pascal, frightened by “the eternal silence of these infinite spaces”, Lucretius with his atoms, and Milton’s angel, who told Adam to leave other worlds to God, are the voices on the other side.
questions: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá argues that so large a universe cannot be empty. Is that an argument from science, from the goodness of God, or from something else?
Pascal found the infinite spaces terrifying; the Psalmist found them a reason for praise. What decides which a person feels?
Milton’s angel says not to trouble about other worlds. Reading 21 warns against speculating about their creatures. How much curiosity do the readings encourage?
What difference would it make to religion if life were found elsewhere?

outside.why: “The creation of God embraceth worlds besides this world.” In my Father’s house are many mansions.
Creatures apart from these creatures. The Qur’an: of His portents is the creation of the heaven and the earth, and of whatever beasts He hath dispersed therein.
Can those great bodies be empty? Of this one Isaiah says: he created it not in vain, he formed it to be inhabited.

Pascal looked at the same sky when the new astronomy had emptied it: the eternal silence of these infinite spaces frightens me. The readings fill those spaces with life. Is that consolation knowledge, or hope?
A question about the planets. Allah it is who hath created seven heavens, and of the earth the like thereof.
The universe is eternal, and life on earth millions of years old. Before the mountains were brought forth, even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God.

Not created “through the fortuitous concurrences of atoms”. The view denied is Lucretius’s, whose first principle was: nothing from nothing ever yet was born. What does the reading’s “great law” add to atoms and chance?
Earth, water and air all have their living beings. Let the waters bring forth abundantly the moving creature that hath life, and fowl that may fly above the earth.
God’s grandeur is shown more by spiritual works than by signs of life on planets. The heavens declare the glory of God; the law of the Lord is perfect, converting the soul.

“It would now be fitting to prepare the means of travel to other planets!” Milton’s angel, asked by Adam about other worlds, discouraged the question: solicit not thy thoughts with matters hid; of other creatures, wherever placed, let Him dispose. Which is the more religious attitude to the stars?
How large is the creation of God! When I consider thy heavens, the work of thy fingers, the moon and the stars, which thou hast ordained; what is man, that thou art mindful of him?
Kant: two things fill the mind with ever new and increasing admiration and awe: the starry heavens above me and the moral law within me.
These matters have not yet been fully discovered. Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding.
Whitman, tired of the lecturer’s proofs and figures, went out and looked up in perfect silence at the stars. What do the readings say astronomy is for?
Each star inhabited. There are more things in heaven and earth, Horatio, than are dreamt of in your philosophy.
This earth, infinitely small, is not empty and purposeless. Blake: to see a World in a Grain of Sand and a Heaven in a Wild Flower.
The planets are of the world of matter, bound by composition and decomposition. The things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal.
Even cotton has feeling. Mountains, and all hills; fruitful trees, and all cedars: praise the Lord from the earth.
Creatures on other planets need not resemble us. He createth that which ye know not.
Other worlds inhabited by beings capable of knowing God. Other sheep I have, which are not of this fold.
The coming of age of this planet. Tennyson’s vision stopped at the Federation of the world.
The greatness of creation, spoken of after morning prayers. These wait all upon thee; thou openest thine hand, they are filled with good.
“All things are alive and living.” Darwin’s closing page: an entangled bank, clothed with many plants of many kinds, with birds singing on the bushes, with various insects flitting about.
The reading is Plotinus; so is this: the One is perfect and, in our metaphor, has overflowed, and its exuberance has produced the new.
Plato’s maker was good and without envy, and wished all things to be like himself. Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights.
All things imitate the First Principle in generosity. Pope’s summary of the old doctrine of plenitude: vast chain of being, which from God began; from infinite to thee, from thee to nothing.
If you can see with the mind’s eye, He will show Himself. Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.
